reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Endocrine Society clinical guidance
clinicalPearls: Occurs in otherwise normally virilised 46,XY males who retain a uterus and fallopian tubes because the anti-mullerian hormone pathway has failed
External genitalia are typically male, since testosterone production and androgen action are intact
Often discovered incidentally at surgery for cryptorchidism or inguinal hernia, where mullerian structures are found in the hernia sac (hernia uteri inguinalis)
Caused by loss-of-function variants in the AMH gene (hormone deficiency) or in its receptor AMHR2 (hormone resistance), inherited in an autosomal recessive manner
Bilateral cryptorchidism and transverse testicular ectopia are common associations
Fertility is frequently impaired owing to undescended testes and disrupted duct anatomy
Undescended testes carry a raised risk of germ cell malignancy, and persistent mullerian remnants require careful surgical judgement to preserve the vas deferens and testicular blood supply
reference.pathophysiology: During normal male development the fetal Sertoli cells secrete anti-mullerian hormone, which acts through the AMHR2 receptor to trigger regression of the mullerian ducts. In persistent mullerian duct syndrome either the hormone is absent (AMH mutations) or its receptor is non-functional (AMHR2 mutations), so the mullerian ducts fail to regress and a uterus and fallopian tubes persist. Because Leydig cell testosterone secretion and androgen signalling are unaffected, wolffian derivatives and the external genitalia develop normally as male. The retained mullerian structures and the frequently maldescended testes distort normal anatomy and impair fertility.
additionalInvestigations: Serum anti-mullerian hormone (low or undetectable in AMH deficiency, normal or high in receptor resistance)
Molecular testing of the AMH and AMHR2 genes
Pelvic and inguinal ultrasound or MRI to identify uterus, tubes and testicular position
Intraoperative identification and, where needed, histology of mullerian remnants
Assessment of testicular function and fertility potential
redFlags: Long-standing intra-abdominal or undescended testes with malignancy risk
An enlarging pelvic or inguinal mass
Surgical injury to the vas deferens or testicular vessels when excising mullerian remnants
Signs of malignant transformation within retained mullerian tissue
reference.prognosis: With orchidopexy and judicious management of mullerian remnants the outlook is generally good, though fertility is often reduced. The principal concerns are testicular malignancy in maldescended gonads and inadvertent damage to reproductive ducts during surgery.
pitfalls: Attempting complete excision of mullerian remnants and injuring the vas deferens or testicular vessels
Failing to recognise mullerian structures found unexpectedly at hernia or orchidopexy surgery
Overlooking the malignancy risk of retained intra-abdominal testes
Confusing the condition with a disorder of androgen action given the normal male phenotype
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guidance on disorders of sex development
management: Orchidopexy to bring the maldescended testes into the scrotum and improve accessibility for cancer surveillance
Careful surgical handling of mullerian remnants, preserving the vasa deferentia and testicular blood supply
Long-term surveillance of the testes for malignancy given the history of maldescent
Assess and counsel on fertility, which is frequently impaired
Maintain the male sex of rearing, as androgen production and action are intact
Genetic counselling and family screening for the autosomal recessive AMH or AMHR2 defect
Coordinate paediatric surgery or urology, endocrinology and clinical genetics
